The exposed data ironically included a vast number of login credential pairs, with one dataset containing 16 collections that held 239,635,000 pairs of emails and passwords. DarkBeam was immediately notified of the vulnerability and secured the exposed interface. While the exposed data was already public from prior breaches, its compilation and organization by DarkBeam created a significant threat by making it more easily accessible. <4> In September 2023, technology and entertainment company Sony became the subject of data breach claims from multiple threat actors. The incident was first publicized on September 25, 2023, when a new extortion group known as RansomedVC claimed to have compromised "all of Sony's systems." [4, 6, 12] The group stated it would sell the stolen data rather than ransom it, alleging Sony was unwilling to pay. [3, 7] RansomedVC posted a small data sample of less than 6,000 files as proof, which was considered unconvincing for a breach of all systems. [4] The situation became more complex when another threat actor, using the alias 'MajorNelson', refuted RansomedVC's claims, calling them "scammers who are just trying to scam you and chase influence." [1, 10, 11] MajorNelson then proceeded to leak a larger 3.14 GB archive of data, which reportedly included all the files from RansomedVC's sample, for free on a hacking forum. [1, 10] Sony acknowledged the situation on September 26, 2023, stating they were investigating the matter but offered no further immediate comment. [3, 10] In early October, Sony clarified that its investigation had identified activity on a single internal test server in Japan and that there was no indication that customer or business partner data was affected, nor was there an adverse impact on operations. [5] <5> The National Student Clearinghouse (NSC), an educational nonprofit, disclosed it was a victim of the widespread MOVEit Transfer software vulnerability, impacting 890 schools across the United States. [3] Unauthorized third-party access to the NSC's MOVEit server occurred around May 30, 2023. [2, 3, 7] While the NSC was alerted to the vulnerability on May 31, 2023, it was not until June 20, 2023, that an investigation confirmed files had been stolen. [1, 2, 9] The compromised data included a wide range of personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, student ID numbers, contact details, and school-related records. [2, 3, 9] The organization filed notifications with various state attorneys general, including in Maine in August and California in September 2023, to announce the full scope of the breach. [3, 9] [5, 6] <6> On September 20, 2023, T-Mobile experienced a temporary system glitch that exposed the personal and financial information of a small number of customers to other users of the T-Mobile app. For a brief period, customers logging into their accounts could see the account details of other individuals, including names, phone numbers, addresses, account balances, and partial credit card information. T-Mobile attributed the issue to a "technology update" and stated that it was not a cyberattack or security breach. The company reported that the glitch affected fewer than 100 customers and was quickly resolved the same day. This incident was separate from other data breaches T-Mobile experienced in 2023, including one in January that affected 37 million customers and another in April impacting a smaller number. Also in September 2023, data from an April breach at a T-Mobile authorized retailer was posted on a hacker forum. <7> Fashion retailer Forever 21 reported a data breach that exposed the personal information of 539,207 current and former employees. [1, 3, 5, 7] An unauthorized third party had intermittent access to the company's systems between January 5, 2023, and March 21, 2023. [2, 3, 6] The company first identified the cyberattack on March 20, 2023, and began sending notification letters to affected individuals on August 29, 2023. [1, 2, 8] The compromised data included names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, bank account numbers (without PINs or access codes), and information related to employee health plans, such as enrollment details and premiums paid. [1, 3, 6, 11] A company spokesperson confirmed the breach did not affect customer data. [1, 3] Forever 21 has stated it has no evidence the stolen data has been misused and is offering complimentary identity theft protection services to the victims. [3, 8] <8> The Rhysida ransomware group was responsible for a significant cyberattack on Prospect Medical Holdings (PMH), a US healthcare company operating 16 hospitals and 166 outpatient centers across California, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, and Rhode Island. The attack, which began on August 3, 2023, caused widespread IT system outages, forcing a reversion to paper-based systems, the suspension of some services including elective surgeries, and the diversion of emergency patients. Rhysida claimed to have stolen 1 terabyte of documents and a 1.3 terabyte SQL database, including over 500,000 Social Security numbers, patient medical records, and other sensitive data, which it later offered for sale on the dark web for 50 bitcoin. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Delta Dental of California and its affiliates confirmed they were impacted by a major data breach stemming from a critical vulnerability in the MOVEit file transfer software. The company discovered the vulnerability on June 1, 2023, and confirmed on July 6, 2023, that personally identifiable information had been stolen. Affecting nearly 7 million (6,928,932) individuals, the attack exposed a wide range of sensitive data, including names, addresses, Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, passport numbers, financial account information, individual health insurance policy numbers, and other health information. Delta Dental began sending notification letters to affected individuals on December 14, 2023, and offered 24 months of complimentary credit monitoring and identity theft protection services. <2> Louisville, Kentucky-based Norton Healthcare experienced a ransomware attack between May 7 and May 9, 2023, which was later claimed by the ALPHV/Blackcat ransomware group. The breach was discovered on May 9, 2023, and resulted in the theft of sensitive data belonging to approximately 2.5 million individuals, including current and former patients, employees, and their dependents. The compromised information included names, contact details, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, health and insurance information, and various identification numbers. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In May 2024, Ticketmaster's parent company, Live Nation, confirmed a significant data breach after identifying unauthorized activity in a third-party cloud database environment on May 20, 2024. [1, 6, 7] A hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility, offering 1.3 terabytes of data allegedly belonging to 560 million customers for sale on the dark web on May 27, 2024. [1, 3, 6] The compromised information reportedly includes customers' full names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, order histories, and partial payment card details. [3, 4, 6] The breach is believed to have originated from the compromise of a Snowflake cloud database account, where hackers gained access using stolen credentials. [1, 2, 3] Live Nation disclosed the incident in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing on May 31, 2024, stating they were investigating the event and cooperating with law enforcement. [1, 6] <2> In late May 2024, Christie's auction house confirmed it had sustained a data breach after initially reporting a "technology security incident" that took its website offline on May 9, 2024. The ransomware group RansomHub claimed responsibility for the attack on May 27, 2024, listing Christie's on its dark web extortion site. RansomHub asserted it had stolen approximately 2GB of sensitive personal information from at least 500,000 of the auction house's international clients, threatening to leak the data unless a ransom was paid. The hackers claimed the data included full names, birth dates, and identification document numbers. Christie's acknowledged that an unauthorized third party had accessed its network and taken a "limited amount of personal data" for some clients but stated there was no evidence that financial or transactional records were compromised. The auction house began notifying affected clients, privacy regulators, and government agencies following the confirmation of the breach. <3> Dell Technologies confirmed it suffered a data breach after a threat actor, known as Menelik, claimed on the Breach Forums cybercrime site on April 28, 2024, that they were selling a database containing information on 49 million customers. The actor allegedly gained access by registering fake partner companies to use a portal API, which they scraped for three weeks starting in March 2024. Dell began notifying affected customers via email around May 8, 2024. The compromised data includes customer names, physical addresses, and Dell hardware and order information, such as service tags, item descriptions, order dates, and warranty details. The company stated that the breach did not expose financial data, payment information, email addresses, or telephone numbers. <4> WebTPA Employer Services, a third-party administrator for health plans, experienced a data breach that compromised the personal information of 2,429,175 individuals. [2, 3, 7] The unauthorized access to WebTPA's network occurred between April 18 and April 23, 2023. [1, 2, 3, 4] However, the suspicious activity was not detected until December 28, 2023. [2, 3, 4, 5, 6] Following an investigation, WebTPA notified its benefit plan and insurance company clients on March 25, 2024, and began issuing data breach notification letters to the affected individuals on May 8, 2024. [2, 3, 4, 9] The compromised data varied by individual but could include names, contact information, dates of birth and death, Social Security numbers, and insurance information. [1, 2, 3, 9] According to WebTPA, financial data such as credit card numbers and information regarding medical treatment or diagnosis were not exposed. [1, 9, 11] The company has offered two years of complimentary identity monitoring services to those impacted. [1, 2, 5] Several class-action lawsuits have been filed against WebTPA, alleging negligence in data security and delays in notifying affected individuals. [2, 6, 8] <5> Kaiser Foundation Health Plan has notified 13.4 million current and former members and patients of a data breach. [2, 4] The incident was not a traditional hack but resulted from online tracking technologies on Kaiser's websites and mobile applications that transmitted sensitive data to third-party vendors like Google, Microsoft Bing, and X. [3] This disclosed information may have included search terms on the company's website, potentially revealing protected health information (PHI). [3] Out of an abundance of caution, Kaiser reported the privacy violation to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office for Civil Rights (OCR) as a potential breach of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). [2, 5]

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Prudential Insurance Company of America provided an update in late June 2024 to a data breach that was initially detected on February 5, 2024. [1, 4, 8] The breach, which occurred on February 4, was initially reported in March as affecting about 36,545 individuals. [1, 4] However, a revised filing with the Maine Attorney General's Office in late June revealed the incident was significantly more extensive, compromising the data of 2,556,210 people. [1, 4, 6] The compromised information includes names, addresses, and driver's license or non-driver identification card numbers. [4, 5, 8] The ransomware group Alphv/BlackCat has claimed responsibility for the attack. [8, 11] Prudential is providing two years of complimentary credit monitoring services to all affected individuals. [1, 4] <2> Infosys McCamish Systems (IMS) formally notified the Maine Attorney General on June 27, 2024, of a significant data breach impacting 6,078,263 individuals. [2, 9] The breach was the result of a ransomware attack allegedly conducted by the LockBit gang, which gained unauthorized access to IMS systems between October 29, 2023, and November 2, 2023. [2, 4] The company first discovered the breach on November 2, 2023, and disclosed the cybersecurity incident in an SEC filing the following day. [2, 9] The LockBit group claimed responsibility on November 4, 2023, stating they had exfiltrated 50 GB of data. [3, 4] Compromised information varied by person but included sensitive data such as names, Social Security numbers, financial account information, medical records, and passport numbers. [2, 3] <3> Evolve Bank & Trust publicly confirmed on June 26, 2024, that it was the victim of a ransomware attack perpetrated by the cybercriminal group LockBit, which resulted in a data breach affecting 7,640,112 individuals. [10, 6] The attackers initially gained access to the bank's systems in February 2024 and again in May, after an employee reportedly clicked a malicious link. [4, 7] The primary data exfiltration occurred around May 29, 2024, with the unauthorized activity being contained by May 31, 2024. [6, 5] The compromised data, which included customer names, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and contact information, was subsequently released on the dark web after Evolve refused to pay the ransom. [5, 7] The breach also impacted customers of Evolve's fintech partners, such as Affirm and Wise. [2, 8] Evolve began notifying affected individuals on July 8, 2024, and offered two years of credit monitoring services. [9, 6] <4> Neiman Marcus Group confirmed it was the victim of a data breach that impacted 64,472 individuals after an unauthorized party accessed its Snowflake cloud database platform. [1, 2, 7] The breach, which occurred between April and May 2024, was part of a broader series of attacks targeting Snowflake customers. [4, 6] The company discovered the intrusion in May 2024 and began sending notification letters to affected customers on June 24, 2024. [2, 5] Compromised data varied by person but included names, contact information, dates of birth, and Neiman Marcus or Bergdorf Goodman gift card numbers; however, gift card PINs were not exposed. [5, 7, 8] Following the disclosure, a hacker known as 'Sp1d3r' offered a database for sale for $150,000, claiming it contained far more extensive data on millions of users and that Neiman Marcus had refused to pay a ransom; these claims have not been officially verified. [2, 3, 5] Neiman Marcus stated it contained the breach by disabling platform access, launching an investigation with cybersecurity experts, and notifying law enforcement. [2, 7] <5> In June 2024, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) confirmed it was investigating a potential data breach after a threat actor named IntelBroker claimed on a hacking forum to be selling stolen company data. The alleged breach reportedly occurred in June 2024. The data for sale purportedly includes sensitive information such as details on future AMD products, source code, firmware, financial records, and databases of both customers and employees. The employee database allegedly contains user IDs, full names, job functions, phone numbers, and email addresses. AMD stated it was working with law enforcement and a third-party hosting partner to investigate the claim, suggesting the data may have originated from a vendor rather than its own systems. In a later update, AMD indicated that its preliminary investigation suggests a limited amount of information related to specifications for assembling certain products was accessed from a third-party site, and the company does not believe the breach will have a material impact on its business. <6> Santander Holdings U.S.A., Inc. began notifying 12,786 of its U.S. employees on June 18, 2024, about a data breach that occurred after an unauthorized party accessed a third-party database. [2, 6] The incident, which the bank identified on May 10, 2024, is believed to have started on April 17, 2024. [3, 4] The compromised records contained sensitive personal information, including employees' names, Social Security numbers, and bank account details used for payroll. [1, 4] This breach is linked to a wider series of attacks targeting customers of the cloud storage provider Snowflake. [4, 5] Santander stated that upon learning of the issue, it blocked access to the affected system and has been in contact with regulators and law enforcement. [1, 8] <7> Ascension, one of the largest non-profit healthcare systems in the U.S., detected a ransomware attack on May 8, 2024, after an employee inadvertently downloaded a malicious file. [3] The attack, believed to be conducted by the cybercriminal group Black Basta, disrupted clinical operations across its facilities. [3, 6] Key systems, including the MyChart electronic health records platform, phones, and various systems for ordering tests, procedures, and medications, were taken offline. [3, 6] This forced a reliance on manual paper-based systems, caused the rescheduling of non-emergent procedures, and led to the diversion of emergency medical services at some hospitals. [3, 4] In a June 13, 2024, update, Ascension confirmed that the attackers had exfiltrated files containing patient and employee data. [2] [7, 9] <8> U.S. food chain Panera Bread experienced a ransomware attack that led to a significant data breach and a week-long nationwide outage of its IT systems. While some sources indicate the breach itself occurred on February 9, 2024, the company officially detected the unauthorized access on March 23, 2024. The attack impacted internal IT systems, point-of-sale systems, phones, and the company's website and mobile apps. An investigation that concluded on May 16, 2024, confirmed that the attackers stole sensitive personal information of current and former employees, including their full names and Social Security numbers. Panera began notifying affected employees around June 13, 2024, and offered one year of credit monitoring services. Following the incident, Panera is facing multiple class-action lawsuits alleging the company failed to properly secure employee data. While no ransomware group has claimed responsibility, speculation from an alleged employee and the wording of an internal email suggest Panera may have paid a ransom with assurances that the stolen data would be deleted. <9> In May 2024, Ticketmaster's parent company, Live Nation, confirmed a significant data breach after identifying unauthorized activity in a third-party cloud database environment on May 20, 2024. [1, 6, 7] A hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed responsibility, offering 1.3 terabytes of data allegedly belonging to 560 million customers for sale on the dark web on May 27, 2024. [1, 3, 6] The compromised information reportedly includes customers' full names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, order histories, and partial payment card details. [3, 4, 6] The breach is believed to have originated from the compromise of a Snowflake cloud database account, where hackers gained access using stolen credentials. [1, 2, 3] Live Nation disclosed the incident in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing on May 31, 2024, stating they were investigating the event and cooperating with law enforcement. [1, 6] <10> In late May 2024, Christie's auction house confirmed it had sustained a data breach after initially reporting a "technology security incident" that took its website offline on May 9, 2024. The ransomware group RansomHub claimed responsibility for the attack on May 27, 2024, listing Christie's on its dark web extortion site. RansomHub asserted it had stolen approximately 2GB of sensitive personal information from at least 500,000 of the auction house's international clients, threatening to leak the data unless a ransom was paid. The hackers claimed the data included full names, birth dates, and identification document numbers. Christie's acknowledged that an unauthorized third party had accessed its network and taken a "limited amount of personal data" for some clients but stated there was no evidence that financial or transactional records were compromised. The auction house began notifying affected clients, privacy regulators, and government agencies following the confirmation of the breach.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On May 28, 2025, data analytics firm LexisNexis Risk Solutions officially disclosed a data breach that impacted 364,333 individuals. The breach resulted from an unauthorized third party acquiring data held in the company's GitHub account, which is used for software development. The compromised personally identifiable information included individuals' names, contact information (such as phone number, postal or email address), Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and dates of birth. While the company began sending data breach notifications to affected people starting May 24, 2025, the disclosure was officially filed with the Maine Attorney General's Office and widely reported on May 28, 2025. <2> Alera Group, an independent national insurance and financial services firm, reported a significant data breach resulting from a hacking incident. The unauthorized access to Alera Group's technology environment occurred between July 19, 2024, and August 4, 2024. The company detected the suspicious activity in August 2024 and completed its investigation on April 28, 2025, confirming that sensitive information had been compromised. There are conflicting reports on the number of individuals affected; a report to the HHS' Office for Civil Rights stated 155,567 individuals were impacted, while a filing with the Maine Attorney General's office mentioned 10,874 people. The compromised data varies by individual but could include names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, driver's licenses, financial and credit card information, passport details, and protected health information (PHI) such as medical history, diagnosis, and insurance data. Alera Group began issuing notification letters to potentially affected individuals on May 21, 2025, and is offering 24 months of complimentary credit monitoring services. <3> Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase confirmed a data breach impacting 69,461 users, which stemmed from an insider threat. [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] The incident began on December 26, 2024, when criminals bribed overseas customer support contractors, reportedly based in India, to exfiltrate sensitive user data. [6, 7] The stolen information included names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, masked Social Security and bank account numbers, government ID images, and account balance details. [5, 6] The breach was discovered by Coinbase on May 11, 2025, the same day the company received and rejected a $20 million extortion demand from the perpetrators. [3, 6, 7] Coinbase stated that passwords and private keys were not compromised. [3, 6] The company has since terminated the involved employees, is cooperating with law enforcement, and offered a reward for information leading to the arrest of the attackers. [1, 6] <4> In April 2025, a threat actor identified as 'l33tfg' claimed to have breached PJM Interconnection LLC, which is North America's largest electric transmission system operator. The actor alleged the breach affected over 4,000 customer database entries, with leaked data purportedly including names, email addresses, and phone numbers. This critical infrastructure target raises significant energy security concerns. There has been no official confirmation from PJM Interconnection regarding the breach. Reports on the incident from April 30, 2025, note that investigations were likely underway. <5> The Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC) announced on April 30, 2025, that it was notifying an additional 33,529 state benefits recipients that their private information was improperly accessed by nine state employees. [1, 2, 3] This action followed a previously announced privacy breach from January 17, 2025, which had initially affected approximately 61,000 individuals, bringing the total number of affected people to around 94,000. [3, 4] The compromised data included protected health, personal identifying, or sensitive personal information. [2, 3] The nine employees involved were terminated for accessing the information without a valid business reason. [2, 3] HHSC began sending notification letters via first-class mail to the newly identified individuals on April 30, 2025. [2] <6> In late April and May 2025, Ascension, a major non-profit U.S. health system, announced a series of data breaches originating from third-party vendors. The most significant of these incidents, which occurred in December 2024, exposed the protected health information of 437,329 patients. [1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8] This breach did not compromise Ascension's own systems but stemmed from a vulnerability in the Cleo file transfer software used by a former business partner, to whom Ascension had inadvertently exposed patient data. [4, 6] The compromised information included highly sensitive details such as names, Social Security numbers, contact information, health insurance details, diagnoses, and clinical visit records. [4, 5] Ascension reported the breach to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) on April 28, 2025. [5] This event is distinct from a separate, larger ransomware attack in May 2024 that affected 5.6 million Ascension patients. [2, 3] <7> VeriSource Services, a Houston-based HR outsourcing and employee benefits administration firm, disclosed that a data breach has impacted approximately 4 million individuals, consisting of employees and their dependents from its client companies. The cybersecurity incident was first detected on February 28, 2024, with an investigation revealing that an unauthorized actor had accessed and exfiltrated files on or about February 27, 2024. The exposed data includes sensitive personal information such as full names, addresses, dates of birth, gender, and Social Security numbers. While initial notifications were sent to smaller groups in May and September 2024, the full scope of the breach, affecting 4 million people, was not determined until April 17, 2025, after a lengthy investigation. The company filed a disclosure with the Maine Attorney General's Office on April 23, 2025, and began notifying the wider group of affected individuals, offering them 12 months of free credit monitoring and identity protection services. <8> The Identity Theft Resource Center (ITRC) reported that 824 data compromise events occurred in the first quarter of 2025, impacting over 91.3 million individuals in the United States. [2] This represents a significant increase in the number of victims compared to the 72.5 million affected during the same period in the previous year. Of the 824 compromises, 638 were identified as cyberattacks, 60 resulted from system and human errors, and 11 were physical attacks, with the cause for the remaining 115 being unspecified. [2] The financial services and healthcare sectors were the most affected industries. [2] A notable issue highlighted in the ITRC's analysis is the lack of transparency in breach notifications, with 68% of notices in Q1 2025 failing to provide details about the attack vector. [2]

The breach was discovered on March 22, 2025, with unauthorized access to its network occurring between February 15, 2025, and March 23, 2025. The VanHelsing ransomware group, which emerged in March 2025, claimed responsibility for the attack on March 26, 2025. Compumedics completed its internal investigation on May 13, 2025, and began notifying the affected healthcare providers, which include at least 11 clinics and hospitals, on April 29, 2025. Patients began receiving notification letters around June 27, 2025. <3> Virginia-based logistics company Estes Forwarding Worldwide (EFW), a subsidiary of Estes Express Lines, experienced a cyberattack on May 28, 2025. The ransomware group Qilin claimed responsibility for the attack on June 23, 2025, posting images of allegedly stolen documents, including passports and driver's licenses. EFW publicly confirmed the "cyber event" in late June 2025 and notified customers and employees. According to the company's CEO, Scott Fisher, there was no significant disruption to business, and operations were restored within hours due to existing cybersecurity protocols. The attack did not impact the parent company, Estes Express Lines. An investigation into the incident has been launched, and a law firm is also investigating the potential impact on sensitive personal information. <4> Healthcare SaaS provider Episource, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group's Optum, experienced a ransomware attack where an unauthorized third party accessed its network between January 27, 2025, and February 6, 2025. The breach was detected on February 6, prompting Episource to shut down its systems and notify law enforcement. The company notified the California Attorney General on June 6, 2025, and the Texas Attorney General on June 10, 2025, with public disclosure noted as June 18, 2025. The attack resulted in the exfiltration of sensitive data affecting 5,418,866 U.S. patients. The compromised information included names, Social Security numbers, addresses, dates of birth, contact information, and protected health information such as medical records, diagnoses, test results, and insurance details. While customer notifications began on April 23, 2025, the incident has led to at least one class-action lawsuit alleging inadequate security measures. <5> In early June 2025, the U.S. tax resolution firm Optima Tax Relief became the target of a double-extortion ransomware attack by the 'Chaos' cybercriminal group. The attackers claimed responsibility for the breach on June 6, 2025, when they added Optima Tax Relief to their data leak site. The group asserted they had stolen 69 GB of sensitive information, which included corporate data and client case files containing personal details like Social Security numbers, phone numbers, and addresses. In addition to exfiltrating the data, the 'Chaos' group also encrypted servers within the firm's network. Following the attack, the stolen data was leaked online. The incident prompted at least one law firm to launch an investigation into the data breach on behalf of affected customers. <6> On Thursday, May 29, 2025, the Allentown City School District in Pennsylvania announced that a cyberattack had occurred. This security breach led to the temporary shutdown of the online learning platform, disrupting classes for the day. <7> In early June 2025, The North Face's parent company, VF Corporation, began notifying customers about a credential stuffing attack that was discovered on April 23, 2025. [2, 7, 8] The attack compromised 2,861 customer accounts on thenorthface.com. [1, 10, 11] Attackers used login credentials stolen from other third-party data breaches to gain unauthorized access. [1, 7] The exposed personal information included customers' full names, purchase histories, shipping addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, and dates of birth. [2, 4, 9] However, payment card information was not compromised, as it is handled by a third-party processor and not stored on the website. [1, 2, 8] While the incident occurred amid a series of cyberattacks on other retailers attributed to the 'Scattered Spider' group, sources do not link this specific credential stuffing attack to them. [1, 12, 14] In response, The North Face reset the passwords for all affected accounts. [8, 9] <8> A cyberattack targeting Lorain County, Ohio, first became apparent on Tuesday, May 27, 2025, when a 'cyber incident' was detected at the County Auditor's Office. [4, 6, 7] The situation escalated, and by the evening of Thursday, May 29, county officials publicly announced a broader 'network security incident'. [6] This led to significant disruptions on Friday, May 30, including the closure of the Lorain County Common Pleas Court's General, Domestic Relations, and Juvenile divisions, as well as the Adult Probation offices. [6, 9] While the Auditor's office systems are reportedly separate, the timing fueled speculation about a more widespread attack. [5, 7] A ransomware group known as 'Global' later claimed responsibility, alleging they had stolen private information, including bank account details, from the Auditor's Office. [4, 5] County officials, who brought in third-party cybersecurity experts to investigate, stated that essential services like 911 and the Sheriff's office remained operational. [6, 9] All courts and public offices were reopened by Monday, June 2, 2025, though the investigation into the incident continued. [11] <9> On May 28, 2025, data analytics firm LexisNexis Risk Solutions officially disclosed a data breach that impacted 364,333 individuals. The breach resulted from an unauthorized third party acquiring data held in the company's GitHub account, which is used for software development. The compromised personally identifiable information included individuals' names, contact information (such as phone number, postal or email address), Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and dates of birth. While the company began sending data breach notifications to affected people starting May 24, 2025, the disclosure was officially filed with the Maine Attorney General's Office and widely reported on May 28, 2025. <10> Kettering Health, a nonprofit network of 14 hospitals and over 120 outpatient facilities in Ohio, was the victim of a ransomware attack by the 'Interlock' gang, which was detected on May 20, 2025. The attack prompted an immediate shutdown of IT systems to contain the threat, leading to significant operational disruptions. These included the cancellation of elective inpatient and outpatient procedures, and impacts on phone lines and the Epic electronic health record (EHR) system, forcing staff to revert to manual processes. By June 5, 2025, Kettering Health confirmed the involvement of the Interlock group and announced that the threat had been eradicated from its systems. The ransomware gang claimed to have stolen 941 GB of data, including patient, financial, and employee information, and began leaking it after the health system refused to pay a ransom. Kettering Health began a phased restoration of services, with core components of its EHR back online by June 2 and other services like the MyChart patient portal being restored in the following weeks.

Cyberattacks were the primary cause of breaches in Q3, accounting for the vast majority of incidents and victims. The ITRC noted a concerning trend of breach notifications lacking details about the attack's cause, with 71% of Q3 notices omitting this information. <5> Volvo Group confirmed that personal data of its employees was exposed in a ransomware attack on its Swedish HR software provider, Miljödata. The attack, attributed to the DataCarry ransomware group, began on August 20, 2025, and was detected by Miljödata on August 23, 2025. Volvo Group was notified on September 2, 2025, that the breach impacted its employees. For some U.S. employees of Volvo Group North America, the exposed data included first and last names and Social Security Numbers. Volvo's internal systems were not compromised in the incident. This attack was part of a larger breach that affected approximately 25 private companies and nearly 200 Swedish municipalities. The stolen data was later published on the dark web on September 14, 2025. In response, Volvo Group offered affected employees 18 months of free identity protection and credit monitoring services. <6> Automotive manufacturer Stellantis confirmed a data breach that exposed the contact information of its North American customers. The incident stemmed from unauthorized access to a third-party service provider's platform, which is connected to the company's Salesforce instance. The breach is believed to be part of a wider hacking campaign by the extortion group ShinyHunters, which has targeted numerous companies using Salesforce. Stellantis stated that the compromised data was limited to customer names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses, and did not include any financial or other sensitive personal information. The compromised data was limited to "commonly available business contact information," including names, email addresses, and phone numbers. This attack is believed to be linked to a broader campaign by the cybercrime group ShinyHunters, which has targeted other major companies. <8> Global staffing company Manpower confirmed that its independently owned and operated franchise in Lansing, Michigan, was the victim of a ransomware attack conducted by the RansomHub group. The breach occurred between December 29, 2024, and January 12, 2025. The incident was first detected on January 20, 2025, following an IT outage. On January 22, 2025, the RansomHub ransomware group claimed responsibility, stating they had exfiltrated 500GB of data. The stolen information reportedly included sensitive personal and corporate data such as Social Security numbers, IDs, financials, and contracts. Manpower began notifying the 144,189 affected individuals around August 11-12, 2025, and reported the breach to the FBI. The affected systems include the Case Management/Electronic Case Files (CM/ECF) and the Public Access to Court Electronic Records (PACER), which host confidential court documents. According to anonymous sources, the Judiciary became aware of the incident's full severity around July 4, 2025. While the official announcement from the Judiciary does not explicitly confirm that sensitive documents were breached, it does state that it is taking additional steps to strengthen protections for such documents and is working to mitigate the impact on litigants. A report from Politico, citing anonymous sources, claimed the breach was a sweeping intrusion that may have exposed the identities of confidential informants. In response to the attacks, the Judiciary is enhancing the security of its systems and collaborating with the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. Staff for the House and Senate Judiciary Committees were briefed on the matter on July 23, 2025, and have requested a follow-up classified briefing.
